exhibits.title: Southwestern Skies
exhibits.subtitle: Same sky, distinct traditions and archaeological readings
exhibits.description: A curated walk through public sky stories and archaeological interpretations from the Greater Southwest and the Basin of Mexico, set beside a Same Sky comparison of the Pleiades. Living community traditions that are not already READY and public in Cartography are not invented or filled in.
exhibits.source_note: Public archaeological and historical sources only. Living Diné, Apache, Hopi, Zuni, Acoma, and Taos stories are not included because they are not READY and public in this source pack. Cultural stories and archaeological interpretations remain separate.

steps.title: Cultural astronomy
steps.narration_text: Cultural astronomy is how communities have used the sky for timing, season, orientation, and identity. Living traditions are contemporary knowledge held by communities. Archaeological interpretation is a scholarly reading of sites and alignments. This exhibit keeps those categories separate and does not claim a common origin for the stories shown here.
steps.transition_note: We begin with the Pleiades as one physical sky seen through distinct traditions.

steps.title: Pleiades — same sky, different stories
steps.transition_note: The cluster is one physical object. The traditions remain distinct.

steps.narration_text: Across the cards in this exhibit, the sky is used for timing, season, orientation, and identity. These are independent traditions and archaeological readings of the same physical sky. This exhibit does not claim a shared origin.

steps.title: Sources and further exploration
steps.narration_text: Sources for each step are grouped in the exhibit source panel. You can continue in Stories of the Sky, Archaeoastronomy Visual Mode, or the Sky Time Machine. Official media and Cosmic Signals remain manual in their existing panels.

exhibits.title: Hear the Universe
exhibits.subtitle: What astronomical sound actually means
exhibits.description: A curated walk through real mission signals, audification, Chandra data sonification, pulsar timing, and Cartography's generated Data Sonification. Ordinary acoustic sound needs matter; these clips translate measured electromagnetic, plasma, and image data into a form human ears can follow.
exhibits.source_note: Audio items are Cosmic Signal Deck entries with NASA, Chandra, JPL, Juno Waves, and Voyager provenance. Cartography Data Sonification is a local altitude-to-pitch mapping, not an observatory recording. Nothing here is microphone audio from vacuum.

steps.title: Can space make sound?
steps.narration_text: Ordinary acoustic sound is a pressure wave. It needs matter to travel. Most of space is vacuum, so a microphone would not pick up a roar from Jupiter or a supernova. Spacecraft and telescopes instead measure changing electromagnetic fields, plasma waves, X-rays, and pulse timing. Scientists can map those data into frequencies humans can hear. This exhibit is about translated information, not sound waves crossing empty space.

sound_explainer.title: Can space make sound?
sound_explainer.lead: Ordinary acoustic sound requires matter, but space missions detect many kinds of changing physical signals that can be translated into audible form.

points.label: Pressure waves in matter
points.text: Everyday hearing is air, water, or rock carrying compressions to an ear or microphone. Vacuum cannot carry that kind of sound.

points.label: Plasma waves
points.text: Charged particles around planets and in the solar wind support electromagnetic plasma waves. Instruments record those fields; some frequencies already sit in the human hearing range and can be amplified.

points.label: Radio and electromagnetic measurements
points.text: Radio, magnetic, and electric-field receivers on spacecraft capture changing signals. Published clips convert those measurements into speaker motion. That is not air vibrating at the planet.

points.label: Timing data
points.text: Pulsars repeat on precise clocks. A light curve or pulse train can be played as a beat because the timing itself is the measurement.

points.label: Astronomical data sonification
points.text: Images and spectra can be scanned into pitch, loudness, and time. NASA and Chandra publish some of those mappings. Cartography can also generate a local mapping from numeric sky data. Both are transformations, not original physical audio recordings.

steps.title: Jupiter — Juno Waves bow shock
steps.narration_text: Juno's Waves instrument measured radio and plasma-wave fields as the spacecraft crossed Jupiter's bow shock. The University of Iowa published this clip as an audible conversion of those measurements. You are not hearing atmospheric thunder. Press Play only if you want to listen. A related Juno auroral radio clip is available to open in the Cosmic Signal Deck. It is a separate measurement, not a second copy of this bow-shock signal.

steps.title: Saturn — Chandra and Cassini sonification
steps.narration_text: This Saturn clip is a Chandra data sonification that also uses Cassini optical imagery of the planet and rings. NASA and the Chandra X-ray Center mapped image structure into synthetic tones. It is not a microphone at Saturn, and it is not Enceladus plume audio. Cartography has no separate Enceladus Cosmic Signal; do not treat this clip as the moon. Official Chandra media and the Saturn spectrum view stay manual in their existing panels.

steps.title: Crab Nebula — image sonification and pulsar timing
steps.narration_text: The Crab Pulsar is a spinning neutron star. Its radio and X-ray pulses repeat like a clock, which is why timing data can sound like a beat. The clip on this step is not that pulse train. NASA and Chandra sonified a multiwavelength image of the nebula, scanning left to right and mapping brightness to loudness. A related Chandra sonification of MSH 15-52 includes the pulsar light curve as pulses about seven times per second. Open that related signal in the Cosmic Signal Deck if you want to hear timing mapped explicitly. It is a different object.

steps.title: Cassiopeia A — canonical Chandra sonification
steps.narration_text: Cassiopeia A is the canonical Chandra sonification in Cartography. NASA and the Chandra X-ray Center mapped element distributions and high-energy structure outward from the center. This exhibit uses that exact Cosmic Signal Deck entry and does not add a second player. Official Chandra media and the Spectrum Gallery remain available beside it. Nothing starts until you press Play.

steps.title: Galactic Center — Chandra data sonification
steps.narration_text: NASA and Chandra provide this Galactic Center sonification of Chandra, Hubble, and Spitzer image data, including the region around Sagittarius A star. It is data sonification, not a microphone recording at the black hole. Stellarium in this session cannot select Sagittarius A star itself, so Cartography focuses the verified search name Sagittarius A East, a nearby remnant, while the Cosmic Signal and Spectrum stay on the Galactic Center material.
steps.stellarium_search_note: Sagittarius A* is not selectable in Stellarium 26.3 Remote Control; verified search_name is Sagittarius A East.

steps.title: Andromeda — multiwavelength sonification
steps.narration_text: NASA and Chandra provide this Andromeda Galaxy sonification. Wavelength layers from X-ray through radio are stacked and scanned left to right. Brightness controls volume and vertical position controls pitch. This is telescope-data sonification of M31, not sound recorded in another galaxy. Open the official media and spectrum items if you want the matching visual context. They stay manual.

steps.title: How sonification works
steps.narration_text: Voyager 1's Plasma Wave Subsystem measured electric-field oscillations in interstellar space. Those frequencies already fall in the human hearing range, so NASA amplified them. That is audification of a measured plasma-wave signal, not a musical remix and not a microphone in vacuum. Measured instrument signals, audification, data sonification, pulse timing, and Cartography's generated Data Sonification are different classes. The next step compares an official observatory sonification with Cartography's own mapping.

steps.title: Same data, different sense
steps.narration_text: NASA and Chandra provide the Andromeda sonification you can reopen here. Cartography is generating a different Data Sonification from the current object's computed altitude, mapping numbers onto a four-second oscillator sweep from 220 to 660 hertz. Both can be scientifically meaningful as translations. Their mappings differ. The generated tone is not an original physical audio recording and is not the Chandra clip. Play each one yourself. Official media and Spectrum stay manual.

steps.title: Free listen
steps.narration_text: These remaining Cosmic Signal Deck entries stay under your control. Earth chorus waves are measured magnetospheric plasma signals already in the hearing range. Venus and Europa clips are Parker and Juno instrument conversions. Vela and M87 are Chandra data sonifications of other deep-sky targets. Choose one to open. Nothing plays until you press Play.

steps.title: Hearing information, not vacuum
steps.narration_text: We are not hearing the vacuum itself; we are hearing information from the Universe translated into a form our ears can perceive. Mission teams choose some mappings. Cartography generates another from local numbers. Sources for each signal stay in the exhibit panel and in the Cosmic Signal Deck. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium to the selection and field of view captured when you started.

exhibits.title: Ancient Skywatchers
exhibits.subtitle: How people measured time, seasons, direction, and meaning in the sky
exhibits.description: A curated walk through production-ready Cartography stories and archaeoastronomy visuals about naked-eye observation: horizon and shadow, calendars, architecture, seasonal star timing, named asterisms, and historical cataloging. Traditions and archaeological readings stay distinct. This exhibit does not claim a shared origin.
exhibits.source_note: Public archaeological, historical, and Stellarium sky-culture sources already READY in Cartography. Living Diné, Apache, Hopi, Zuni, Acoma, and Taos stories are not included. Mesa Verde Sun Temple remains RESEARCH_MORE and is omitted. Cultural stories, historical astronomy, and archaeological interpretation remain separate.

steps.title: Before telescopes
steps.narration_text: Careful naked-eye observation can be precise. Horizon points, shadows, repeated star positions, lunar phases, and seasonal cycles were measuring tools. Different societies developed different systems for time, direction, ceremony, navigation, and knowledge. This exhibit keeps each tradition distinct rather than merging them into one ancient people.

steps.title: Reading the horizon
steps.narration_text: Sunrise and sunset do not stand still on the horizon. Over the year they move between recurring solstice extremes, with equinox positions in between. A marked hill, building axis, or shadow path can turn that motion into a calendar. The method is shared in function only where sources support it. The next cards are specific places and traditions, not a universal ancient technique.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Horizon sunrise and sunset positions; repeating seasonal extremes.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: The Sun's rising and setting azimuths return each year to solstice and equinox stations.
how_they_knew.environmental_calendar_role: Seasonal timing without telescopes or spacecraft.
how_they_knew.evidence_type: General observational method. Site-specific claims wait for sourced cards.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: This step does not assign a particular culture's calendar to the current Stellarium Sun.

place_context.region: Wherever a level or marked horizon can be watched

steps.title: Chaco cardinal architecture
steps.narration_text: Archaeological evidence suggests major Chaco buildings were aligned close to the cardinal directions. The visual here is limited to that strong, publicly sourced claim. Lunar-standstill and Casa Rinconada niche-light ideas stay omitted from the primary diagram. This is architectural astronomy, not an oral constellation story.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Building axes laid out near true north–south and east–west.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: Cardinal axes can mark solar noon and equinox sunrises and sunsets on an idealized horizon.
how_they_knew.architectural_relationship: Pueblo Bonito and related Chaco constructions.
how_they_knew.evidence_type: STRONG EVIDENCE for cardinal orientation; archaeological inference.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: Unsupported lunar claims are not treated as settled fact.

place_context.observing_environment: Built architecture on the canyon floor

steps.title: Fajada Butte Sun Dagger
steps.narration_text: This archaeological interpretation of Ancestral Puebloan observations suggests midday light on spiral petroglyphs at Fajada Butte marked the solar year. The diagram is an interpretive schematic, labeled scholarly interpretation. Disputed lunar-standstill claims stay secondary. This is not a living oral tradition.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Sunlight and shadow position on spiral petroglyphs.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: A dagger of light at midday near solstice and equinox, as publicly interpreted.
how_they_knew.architectural_relationship: Fajada Butte slabs and petroglyphs. The site is closed.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: Lunar-standstill readings remain disputed and are not the primary claim.

place_context.observing_environment: Sunlight through rock slabs on Fajada Butte

steps.title: Hovenweep Holly solstice panel
steps.narration_text: Archaeological evidence suggests Ancestral Puebloan observers at Hovenweep marked the summer solstice with a light beam on the Holly petroglyph panel. The relationship is observational and seasonal. It is a scholarly reading of a public NPS interpretation, not a reconstructed ceremony or a living oral story.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: A light beam falling on a petroglyph panel near summer solstice sunrise.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: The summer-solstice sun returns to the same horizon point each year.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: The panel is interpreted as a seasonal marker; Cartography does not reconstruct unstated ritual speech.

steps.title: Mexica solar observation — Templo Mayor
steps.narration_text: This archaeological interpretation of Mexica observations suggests the Templo Mayor and eastern mountain foresights marked solar dates in the agricultural year. In the Mexica historical sources represented here, this is historical Mexica architecture, not a modern Nahua classroom story and not Maya astronomy.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Sunrise along a built axis toward mountain foresights.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: Solar dates in the agricultural year return along the same horizon line.
how_they_knew.architectural_relationship: Templo Mayor / Tenochtitlan and Mount Tlaloc alignments as published.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: This is not generic Mesoamerican mythology.

place_context.observing_environment: Urban temple and eastern mountain horizon

steps.title: Pleiades as a clock — Tianquiztli
steps.narration_text: In the Mexica historical sources represented here, Tianquiztli is identified with the Pleiades and used in calendrical timing, including the New Fire watch. This is historical Mexica language from colonial Nahuatl sources, not a modern Nahua or Maya story. A scientific image of the cluster, if shown, is a NASA view of the same stars. It is not the cultural source.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Pleiades position and timing, including the New Fire watch as sourced.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: The cluster's night-time place in the seasonal calendar.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: Not living classroom instruction and not merged with Maya astronomy.

steps.title: Arabian Peninsula star timing — al-Thurayyā
steps.narration_text: In Arabian Peninsula anwāʾ traditions represented here, al-Thurayyā is a seasonal timing asterism. The knowledge is environmental and calendrical: when a well-known group of stars returns, weather and work can be timed. This is Peninsula folk and anwāʾ star knowledge, distinct from al-Ṣūfī's Book of Fixed Stars and from any collapsed folk category.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Seasonal heliacal rising and setting traditions where the local source pack supports them; anwāʾ star timing.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: The Pleiades return in a seasonal cycle used for environmental knowledge.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: Not a Ptolemaic catalog and not a stand-in for all Arabic-speaking societies.

place_context.period: Anwāʾ / Peninsula oral stellar tradition as documented in the sky-culture pack

steps.title: Māori seasonal sky knowledge — Matariki
steps.narration_text: Within the Māori tradition represented here, Matariki is the name for the Pleiades in Tātai Arorangi, the Māori astronomical tradition documented in this source pack. Public Matariki marking in Aotearoa is contemporary. Variants among iwi are acknowledged and are not merged. This card does not generalize Māori knowledge to all Polynesian traditions.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Seasonal appearance of Matariki as documented in the Māori sky-culture sources used here.
how_they_knew.environmental_calendar_role: Seasonal / new-year sky knowledge; navigation is cited in the source pack without being expanded here.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: Iwi variation is real. This is not a pan-Polynesian summary.

place_context.period: Living tradition; public Matariki marking is contemporary

steps.title: Chinese sky organization — Běi Dǒu
steps.narration_text: In this Chinese Xingguan tradition, Běi Dǒu, the Northern Dipper, is a named seven-star grouping used to organize the northern sky. Xingguan are not IAU constellations, and this card does not treat Běi Dǒu as a Chinese translation of Ursa Major. Cartography does not add unsourced court-astronomy or imperial-ritual detail beyond the sky-culture pack.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Named asterism: a recognized seven-star grouping in the north.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: The same stars remain a stable figure for orientation and sky division.
how_they_knew.astronomical_object: Běi Dǒu / Northern Dipper (primary star Dubhe in Stellarium)
how_they_knew.environmental_calendar_role: Sky organization and orientation. Court astronomy is not claimed here.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: Xingguan are not IAU boundaries. No unsourced imperial office is added.

place_context.period: Chinese Xingguan tradition as documented in the Yixiang Kaocheng / Stellarium Chinese pack

steps.title: Medieval Islamic star cataloging — al-Lawrā
steps.narration_text: In al-Ṣūfī's historical astronomical work, al-Lawrā is the Lyre in the Book of Fixed Stars, around the year 964. That treatise observed, inherited, and revised Ptolemaic star descriptions. This is medieval Islamic mathematical astronomy, not folk mythology, and it is not merged with Arabian Peninsula anwāʾ tradition.

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Stellar observation and catalog comparison in a written astronomical treatise.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: Fixed stars described, compared, and revised across inherited catalogs.
how_they_knew.environmental_calendar_role: Cataloging and description rather than a seasonal work calendar.

steps.title: Same sky — different tools
steps.comparison_note: These are independent methods and traditions. Similar observational function is not a shared origin, shared religion, or identical calendar.

method_comparison.evidence: Archaeological inference; strong evidence only where labeled

method_comparison.watched: Sun on the horizon; Pleiades as Tianquiztli
method_comparison.measured: Agricultural solar dates; New Fire timing

steps.narration_text: The same physical sky is used here in different ways: horizon alignment, seasonal star timing, asterism organization, architecture, cataloging, and calendar watch. Similar observational function does not mean these systems began together, shared a religion, or reached identical sophistication. These traditions remain distinct.

steps.title: Optional historical sky reconstruction

how_they_knew.title: How Did They Know?
how_they_knew.observation_method: Modern astronomical reconstruction of an already sourced date analog.
how_they_knew.repeated_pattern: Equinox solar geometry returns each year.
how_they_knew.architectural_relationship: Chaco cardinal architecture visual already shown.
how_they_knew.evidence_type: ASTRONOMICAL RECONSTRUCTION — not proof of the archaeological reading.
how_they_knew.uncertainty: The date is the published AD 1050 equinox analog. No dramatic extra date is invented.

place_context.observing_environment: Stellarium reconstruction of the sourced date

steps.narration_text: You may apply a modern reconstruction of approximately AD 1050, an equinox analog already attached to the Chaco visual. This uses modern astronomical models to reconstruct the sky. It does not independently prove the archaeological or historical interpretation. A Mexica xiuhmolpilli-year analog exists on the Templo Mayor visual if you open that visual later. Time restores when you exit.

steps.title: Tools of the sky
steps.narration_text: Ancient skywatchers were not all doing the same thing. They used the same sky for different practical, cultural, ceremonial, navigational, and intellectual purposes. Horizon, shadow, cardinal architecture, Pleiades timing, seasonal stars, named asterisms, and written catalogs appear in this exhibit only where Cartography already has production sources. Sources stay grouped in the exhibit panel.

exhibits.title: Light Echoes
exhibits.subtitle: When yesterday's outburst still lights the dust
exhibits.description: Learn how light from a brief astronomical event can illuminate surrounding dust at different times. Interactive illustrative geometry, real documented examples, optional Stellarium focus, and user-controlled narration.
exhibits.source_note: Scientific outreach exhibit. Geometry controls are ILLUSTRATIVE educational simplifications, not measured 3D reconstructions. Imagery cites ESA/Hubble and Chandra public pages. Distinct from cultural Stories of the Sky.

steps.title: What is a light echo?
steps.narration_text: A light echo is delayed starlight. A brief flash races outward, strikes dust that was already there, and only then heads toward us. What you watch expanding on the sky is mostly the illumination front, not a cloud flying apart at that speed.

steps.title: Source, dust, observer
steps.narration_text: Picture three points: the transient source, a dust sheet, and the observer. The straight path is shortest. Any bounce adds travel time. Use the Light Echoes Lab time control to watch different dust patches light up as longer paths finally arrive. The diagram is labeled ILLUSTRATIVE—not a measured reconstruction.

steps.title: Apparent expansion
steps.narration_text: If the glow seems to grow faster than light, remember: nothing physical is sprinting that fast. Different sightlines simply deliver the reflected flash on different schedules. Advance the illustrative timeline to see nearer and farther dust light in sequence.

steps.title: V838 Monocerotis
steps.narration_text: In 2002, V838 Monocerotis brightened dramatically. Hubble later imaged a spectacular light echo as the outburst illuminated surrounding dust. Focus the object in Stellarium when available, and open the curated ESA/Hubble image in the Light Echoes Lab.

steps.title: Cassiopeia A light echoes
steps.narration_text: Cassiopeia A preserves both a spectacular remnant and documented light echoes that illuminate dust long after the explosion. Keep remnant structure distinct from light-echo dust while you inspect the scientific media and Stellarium focus.

steps.title: SN 1987A
steps.narration_text: SN 1987A produced famous circumstellar rings whose brightening is governed by light-travel time. Ring material was already there; the delayed glow teaches the same geometry as classic light echoes.

steps.title: Takeaway
steps.narration_text: Light echoes teach patience and geometry: yesterday's outburst can still sculpt today's sky, revealing dust we would otherwise never see. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium to the selection and field of view captured when you started.

exhibits.title: Cosmic Web
exhibits.subtitle: Galaxies, filaments, nodes, and voids
exhibits.description: How gravity grows the large-scale cosmic web from tiny early density differences. Interactive illustrative lab, survey and simulation media with explicit classification badges, and Stellarium sky anchors for nearby structures.
exhibits.source_note: Scientific outreach. Interactive lab is ILLUSTRATIVE. Media cards are labeled OBSERVATION, RECONSTRUCTION, SIMULATION, or ILLUSTRATION. Stellarium is a sky anchor only.

steps.title: The Universe is not random
steps.narration_text: Look past single galaxies. On the largest scales, matter forms a cosmic web: bright nodes, connecting filaments, and enormous quiet voids.

steps.title: From small differences
steps.narration_text: In the early Universe the density field was nearly smooth, with tiny ripples. Those ripples were enough for gravity to work with. Advance the illustrative timeline from nearly uniform toward first clumps.

steps.title: Gravity builds structure
steps.narration_text: Gravity amplified small overdensities. Dark matter provided most of the scaffolding mass; ordinary matter followed into the wells and lit up as galaxies. The lab remains an ILLUSTRATIVE diagram, not a measured map.

steps.title: Galaxies form groups
steps.narration_text: Groups are denser than the field but smaller than rich clusters. The Local Group—home to the Milky Way and Andromeda—is our nearest group-scale example. Stellarium can focus Andromeda as a sky anchor.

steps.title: Filaments connect them
steps.narration_text: Matter streams into elongated ridges—filaments—that stitch denser regions together. Toggle filaments in the Cosmic Web Lab to see this ILLUSTRATIVE stage.

steps.title: Nodes and clusters
steps.narration_text: Filament intersections grow into nodes that host groups and clusters. Virgo, anchored here via M87, is a nearby rich concentration—seen on the sky, not as a full 3D web inside Stellarium.

steps.title: A classic rich node — Coma
steps.narration_text: The Coma Cluster is a textbook rich node. Stellarium can focus it directly while survey media remind us that Coma is one patch inside a vastly larger reconstructed web.

steps.title: The great voids
steps.narration_text: Between the filaments, underdense regions grew into great voids—comparatively quiet and sparse. Toggle voids in the ILLUSTRATIVE lab to complete the mature web picture.

steps.title: Real surveys reconstruct the web
steps.narration_text: We do not photograph the entire cosmic web as one object. Redshift surveys such as SDSS and DESI map millions of galaxies in 3D. Those maps are observational reconstructions—clearly labeled apart from the lab illustration and from simulations.

steps.title: Simulations grow webs in computers
steps.narration_text: Cosmological simulations evolve matter under gravity from early fluctuations into filamentary webs. They are calculations labeled SIMULATION—not photographs—and help interpret what surveys find.

steps.title: Fragments of the web overhead
steps.narration_text: From a nearly smooth beginning, gravity built today's cosmic architecture. Surveys map it; simulations explain it; Stellarium shows nearby fragments of it overhead. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium to the capture from when you started.

exhibits.title: Gravitational Waves
exhibits.subtitle: A new sense for the Universe
exhibits.description: Interactive walk through spacetime ripples, LIGO-class interferometers, chirps, GW150914, detector networks, GW170817, and multi-messenger astronomy. Labs are illustrative; event cards cite LIGO/Virgo and observatory sources.
exhibits.source_note: Wave/interferometer labs ILLUSTRATIVE with exaggerated strain. Chirp tones are ILLUSTRATIVE SONIFICATIONS. Event references: LIGO/Virgo publications and ESO/Hubble host imaging.

steps.title: Ripples in spacetime
steps.narration_text: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime itself. They are not sound in air, and they are not a rubber sheet you can grab—they are tiny, traveling changes in distance.

steps.title: What makes a gravitational wave?
steps.narration_text: Accelerating masses with changing quadrupole moments can radiate gravitational waves. Compact binaries—black holes and neutron stars—are the stars of the current detector band.

steps.title: Stretch and squeeze
steps.narration_text: Use the wave lab to compare plus and cross polarizations. Remember: deformations are ILLUSTRATIVE and greatly exaggerated—real strains at Earth are about 10 to the minus 21.

steps.title: How LIGO measures the almost impossible
steps.narration_text: Laser light splits into perpendicular kilometer-scale arms and recombines. A passing wave changes the relative optical path lengths enough—just barely—for a sensitive photodetector to notice.

steps.title: Binary inspiral
steps.narration_text: As a compact binary loses energy to gravitational waves, the orbit tightens and the wave frequency climbs toward merger.

steps.title: Hear the chirp
steps.narration_text: Advance the chirp slider and optionally play the browser tone. That tone is an ILLUSTRATIVE SONIFICATION—frequency-shifted for human ears—not detector-band audio and not sound traveling through space.

steps.title: GW150914
steps.narration_text: GW150914 was the first direct detection: a binary black-hole merger observed by LIGO in September 2015. There is no honest single Stellarium host for its broad localization region.

steps.title: Finding the source
steps.narration_text: Hanford, Livingston, Virgo, and KAGRA form a network. Timing and antenna patterns constrain a sky probability region—often many square degrees—not always a pinpoint.

steps.title: GW170817
steps.narration_text: GW170817 was a binary neutron-star merger with a three-detector gravitational-wave signal and an electromagnetic counterpart in NGC 4993. Stellarium can focus that host galaxy as sky context.

steps.title: Multi-messenger astronomy
steps.narration_text: Waves plus gamma rays, optical/infrared kilonova light, X-rays, and radio together revealed physics neither messenger could give alone—from nuclear matter to cosmic expansion.

steps.title: A new sense for the Universe
steps.narration_text: We now listen to spacetime as well as to light. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium to the capture from when you started.

exhibits.title: Black Holes
exhibits.subtitle: A window on extreme gravity
exhibits.description: Interactive walk through event horizons, Schwarzschild scale, approach regions, illustrative lensing, accretion appearance, tidal forces, EHT imaging of M87* and Sgr A*, Cygnus X-1, and how astronomers detect black holes.
exhibits.source_note: Scale, approach, and lensing labs are ILLUSTRATIVE. Schwarzschild numbers assume non-rotating models unless noted. EHT images are interferometric reconstructions. Stellarium is sky context only.

steps.title: The darkest objects
steps.narration_text: Black holes are regions where spacetime curvature prevents light from escaping beyond an event horizon. This walk separates observation, reconstruction, simulation, illustration, and theoretical models.

steps.title: Gravity without escape
steps.narration_text: A black hole is defined by causal structure—not a solid crust. Rubber-sheet metaphors are only metaphors.

steps.title: The event horizon
steps.narration_text: The horizon is a boundary in spacetime. The singularity of classical general relativity is not directly imaged. The Event Horizon Telescope shadow is larger than the horizon itself.

steps.title: How big is a black hole?
steps.narration_text: Compare stellar-mass and supermassive Schwarzschild radii. Real astrophysical black holes may rotate—labels state the non-rotating teaching assumption.

steps.title: Falling toward the horizon
steps.narration_text: Move through distant space, the accretion region, the photon-orbit region, and the event horizon. The photon sphere is not a solid shell, and you cannot hover freely at the horizon.

steps.title: Light bends
steps.narration_text: Near a black hole, light paths bend. This lab is illustrative relativistic lensing—not a precision ray-tracer—while EHT images reconstruct real interferometric data.

steps.title: Accretion and the glowing disk
steps.narration_text: Bright disks and jets live outside the horizon. Doppler boosting, gravitational redshift, and light bending shape appearance in ray-traced visualizations.

steps.title: Tidal forces
steps.narration_text: Spaghettification is not universal at every horizon. Stellar-mass tides near the horizon can be extreme; for large supermassive black holes, local tides at the horizon can be gentler.

steps.title: Sgr A* — our Galactic Center
steps.narration_text: Sagittarius A-star is the Milky Way’s central supermassive black hole. Stellarium anchors near the Galactic Center using NGC 6522 as honest host-sky context—not a fake Sgr A-star catalog object.

steps.title: M87* — seeing the shadow
steps.narration_text: M87-star gave us the first horizon-scale image in 2019. The dark center is a reconstructed shadow shaped by light bending—not a photograph of a black surface.

steps.title: Stellar-mass black holes
steps.narration_text: Cygnus X-1 is a classic stellar-mass black-hole X-ray binary. Stellarium focuses the optical companion HD 226868—sky context for the system, not a resolved black-hole image.

steps.title: How we know they’re there
steps.narration_text: We find black holes through stellar orbits, X-ray binaries, gravitational waves, Galactic-Center dynamics, and Event Horizon Telescope imaging. Visit the Gravitational Waves Special for chirps and mergers.

steps.title: A window on extreme gravity
steps.narration_text: Black holes reshape light and matter around them. Distinguishing illustration from reconstruction keeps the science honest. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium when you are done.

exhibits.title: Galactic Encounters
exhibits.subtitle: Galaxies grow by meeting
exhibits.description: Interactive walk through tidal forces, tails and bridges, stars versus gas, Antennae, Whirlpool, Mice, major versus minor mergers, remnants, and the uncertain Milky Way–Andromeda future.
exhibits.source_note: Encounter labs ILLUSTRATIVE. Observed systems use ESA/Hubble media. MW–M31 section is FUTURE PREDICTION / SIMULATION and model-dependent.

steps.title: Galaxies are not islands
steps.narration_text: Galaxies influence one another across millions of light-years. This walk separates observation, simulation, illustration, and future prediction.

steps.title: Gravity across millions of light-years
steps.narration_text: Gravity is the main handshake. Dark-matter halos dominate the mass and steer long orbits between galaxies.

steps.title: First passage
steps.narration_text: Advance the encounter lab from approach through first passage. A flyby does not finish a merger overnight—timescales are hundreds of millions to billions of years.

steps.title: Tidal tails and bridges
steps.narration_text: Differential gravity stretches disks: the near side feels a stronger pull than the far side. Tails and bridges are the long signatures of that stretch.

steps.title: Stars mostly miss
steps.narration_text: When galaxies overlap, stars almost never smash into each other. Stellar separations dwarf stellar sizes.

steps.title: Gas collides
steps.narration_text: Gas clouds can compress and shock, helping light new stars. Not every encounter makes the same starburst.

steps.title: The Antennae
steps.narration_text: NGC 4038 and 4039 are a classic merger with long tidal antennae and intense star formation. Hubble imaging is an observation; the lab remains illustrative.

steps.title: The Whirlpool
steps.narration_text: M51 and its companion show how interactions can help organize spiral structure while the pair continues to dance.

steps.title: The Mice
steps.narration_text: NGC 4676 flaunts twin tidal tails—visual proof of strong tidal stripping during an encounter.

steps.title: Major vs minor mergers
steps.narration_text: Major mergers scramble peers of similar mass. Minor mergers let large galaxies grow by absorbing smaller ones, often leaving streams or shells.

steps.title: What remains
steps.narration_text: Remnants are diverse: disturbed disks, elliptical-like shapes, rebuilt gas-rich disks, starbursts, or AGN if fuel reaches the central black hole. Visit Black Holes for horizon-scale physics.

steps.title: Milky Way meets Andromeda?
steps.narration_text: Andromeda approaches on billion-year timescales. Label this FUTURE PREDICTION slash SIMULATION: exact timing and geometry remain model-dependent.

steps.title: Galaxies grow by encounter
steps.narration_text: From Antennae tails to our own Local Group future, encounters write galaxy history. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium when you are done.

exhibits.title: Cosmic Dawn
exhibits.subtitle: The Universe grows up
exhibits.description: Interactive walk from recombination and the CMB through the dark ages, first stars and galaxies, reionization, JWST's early-galaxy frontier, and the cautious 21-cm radio search.
exhibits.source_note: Timeline epochs are approximate. First-star and reionization details remain research frontiers. 21-cm claims stay conservative. Stellarium is present-day optical sky only.

steps.title: Looking back in time
steps.narration_text: Deep sky observing is time travel. Cosmic Dawn is when the first stars ended the dark ages after the Big Bang's afterglow.

steps.title: The Universe becomes transparent
steps.narration_text: Recombination joined electrons to nuclei. Photons stopped scattering endlessly, and light could travel freely.

steps.title: The oldest light
steps.narration_text: Those freed photons are today's cosmic microwave background. Stellarium cannot show the microwave sky—use the Planck map card.

steps.title: The cosmic dark ages
steps.narration_text: After the CMB and before stars, the Universe was dark to starlight but not empty—neutral gas and growing dark-matter structure.

steps.title: Gravity keeps working
steps.narration_text: Tiny density differences grew under gravity. This early structure growth foreshadows the Cosmic Web Special.

steps.title: The first stars ignite
steps.narration_text: First stars formed from primordial gas. Their exact masses remain uncertain—simulation visuals are not photographs of Population III stars.

steps.title: The first galaxies
steps.narration_text: Gas collapsed in dark-matter halos into early galaxies. Mergers and accretion increased complexity—see also Galactic Encounters.

steps.title: Lighting the fog
steps.narration_text: Ionizing radiation carved bubbles in neutral hydrogen. Advance the reionization lab to watch the illustrative fog clear.

steps.title: Reionization
steps.narration_text: Bubbles grew and overlapped until most intergalactic hydrogen was ionized. Exact sources and timing remain active research.

steps.title: JWST opens the frontier
steps.narration_text: JWST finds highly redshifted galaxies. Photometric candidates need careful confirmation—avoid hard-coded earliest-ever claims.

steps.title: Listening for neutral hydrogen
steps.narration_text: The 21-centimeter line could probe the dark ages and reionization, but foregrounds make detection extraordinarily hard. Claims stay conservative.

steps.title: From dawn to the Cosmic Web
steps.narration_text: Deep fields reveal distant galaxies along the path to today's Cosmic Web. Stellarium anchors the Fornax host-sky region, not the early Universe itself.

steps.title: The Universe grows up
steps.narration_text: From microwave afterglow to first firelight, Cosmic Dawn completes this Specials series. Exit and Restore returns Stellarium when you are done.
